entries.23985597901256f41111ea1598e8c0ef9e5da51b: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.13.23" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.13.23" sID="gen97654" type="section"/> <div sID="gen97655" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.13.23">Luke 13:23</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And one saith to him</hi> Although Matthew relates this answer, as if it were immediately connected with other sentences taken out of our Lord’s sermons, yet I rather think that the occasion of its being spoken arose out of the present question. The reason why the question was put appears to have been, that Christ, who declared himself to be the author of life, could with difficulty collect a small number of disciples. It might appear, that a small band of men was to be saved, and that the whole church was going to ruin: for the whole of that nation, among whom the doctrine of Christ made no great progress, and by whom it was universally rejected, had been adopted by God as the heir of life. A similar doubt steals upon us, when we look at the melancholy condition of the world. <hi type="italic">“‘</hi>The greater part of men pursue a life which is utterly at variance with the Gospel. What is the meaning of this?” For this reason Christ, directing his discourse to all, exhorted them to <hi type="italic">strive to enter by the narrow gate</hi> These words were intended to withdraw his people from a foolish curiosity, by which many are retarded and involved, when they look around to see if any companions are joining them, as if they were unwilling to be saved but in a crowd. When he bids them <hi type="italic">strive, </hi>or labor, he conveys the information, that it is impossible to obtain eternal life without great and appalling difficulties. Let believers, therefore, give their earnest attention to this object, instead of indulging in excessive curiosity about the vast number of those who are going astray.<div eID="gen97655" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.13.23" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen97654" osisID="Luke.13.23" type="section"/>
entries.f49350172df561f3ab35079851aaf55e77d4cf4b:
24. For many will seek to enter This was added, that we might not be deceived by a vain hope, as if the multitude of our companions would be of any avail to us. The flesh is willing to flatter itself, and many who now give themselves every indulgence, promise to themselves an easy entrance into life. Thus men practice mutual deception on each other, and fall asleep in wicked indifference. To shake off from his own people those flattering hopes, Christ declares that those who calculate that their possession of life is already certain, will be shut out.
Our author appears to have become apprehensive that this language was ambiguous, and, lest it might be interpreted differently from what he intended, he has taken care to insert in the French Version an explanatory clause: “que ceux qui se font accroire qu'ils sont desia tout asseurez de la vie eternelle, et cheminent a leur plaisir sans souci, en seront rejettez;” —”that those who make themselves believe that they are already perfectly assured of eternal life, and walk on at their pleasure without concern, will be excluded from it.” — Ed.
LUKE 13:25-30
Luke 13:25-30
25. And when the master of the house shall have arisen, and shall have shut the door, and you shall begin to stand without and to knock at the door, saying, Lord, Lord, open to us: and he answering shall say to you, I know not whence you are: 26. Then you shall begin to say, We have eaten and drunk in thy presence, and thou hast taught in our streets. 27. And he shall say, I say to you, I know not whence you are: depart from me, all who work iniquity. 28. Weeping and gnashing of teeth shall be there, when you shall see Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, and all the prophets, in the kingdom of God, and yourselves shut out. 29. And they shall come from the east and west, and north and south, and shall sit down in the kingdom of God. 30. And, lo, they are last who shall be first, and they are first who shall be last.
entries.f19d16e63f4c4bfb984510e3edc32eec90c34759: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.13.25" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.13.25" sID="gen97664" type="section"/> <div sID="gen97665" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.13.25">Luke 13:25</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And when the master of the house shall have arisen</hi> Though these words, as I hinted a little before, were spoken on a different and later occasion, I have chosen to pay more regard to the doctrine than to the time: for it is no slight assistance to the understanding to read, in immediate connection, those passages which are closely related in meaning. As Christ had declared that to many, who shall desire to enter into heaven, the door will not be open, he now asserts, that they gain nothing by occupying a place in the church because God will at length arise in judgment, and shut out from his kingdom those who now lay claim to a place in his family. He employs the comparison of the <hi type="italic">master of a house, </hi>who, having learned that some wicked and dissolute persons among his own domestics steal out unperceived during the night, and expose the house to thieves, <hi type="italic">rises and shuts the door, </hi>and does not allow those night-prowlers to enter, who have been wandering through the public streets at unseasonable hours. By these words he warns us, that we must avail ourselves of the opportunity, while it is offered: for so long as the Lord invites us to himself, the <hi type="italic">door</hi> is, as it were, open, that we may enter into the kingdom of heaven: but the greater part do not deign to move a step. Christ therefore threatens, that <hi type="italic">the door</hi> will at length be <hi type="italic">shut, </hi>and that those who are looking for companions are in danger of being refused admission.<div eID="gen97665" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.13.25" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen97664" osisID="Luke.13.25" type="section"/>
entries.da1ccd6be7ccd2c23cca066acad7e350dfb439da: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.13.26" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.13.26" sID="gen97666" type="section"/> <div sID="gen97667" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">26. </hi><hi type="italic">Thou hast taught in our streets</hi> Christ expressly states, that it will be of no advantage to the Jews, that he approached near to them, and permitted them to enjoy familiar intercourse with him, if, when called, they do not answer at the appointed day. But he does not follow out his comparison: for, after having spoken about <hi type="italic">the master of a house, </hi>he now states, without a figure, that he is himself the judge; and indeed the words, <hi type="italic">thou hast taught in our streets, </hi>can apply to no one but himself. We now perceive his design, which was, to warn the Jews not to allow themselves to lose, by their own neglect, the salvation which it is in their power to obtain.<div eID="gen97667" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.13.26" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen97666" osisID="Luke.13.26" type="section"/>
entries.e6b90979ede58be51c804fe1c95515af01acad4c: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.13.28" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.13.28" sID="gen97668" type="section"/> <div sID="gen97669" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">28. </hi><hi type="italic">When you shall see Abraham</hi> The Jews bore no resemblance to the holy fathers, and had no right to boast of being descended from them: yet nothing was more customary than to abuse the title of the Church. <note n="474"> <div sID="gen97670" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et avoyent tousjours en la bouche le titre d'Eglise, duquel ils abu- soyent</foreign>;” — “and had always in their mouth the title of Church, which they abused.”<div eID="gen97670" type="x-p"/> </note> Christ here assures them, that a bastard race, which has departed from the faith and piety of the fathers, has “no inheritance in <hi type="italic">the kingdom of God,” </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.5.5">Ephesians 5:5</reference>.) There is a silent but implied reproof, that those who were desirous to have companions in seeking salvation, did not endeavor to associate themselves with <hi type="italic">Abraham, and the prophets, </hi>and the holy fathers, instead of looking around among their contemporaries, who had degenerated greatly from their example into innumerable corruptions. “If you neglect (says he) to <hi type="italic">enter by the strait gate, </hi>because you are kept back by the great number of those who are going astray, do you not see that you are separated from the number of believers, and become involved with unbelievers?” If the aspect of the world now dazzles your eyes, the last day will cure you of this folly, but it will be too late: for you shall then know that you, and others like you, are excluded from <hi type="italic">the kingdom of God, </hi>and have no part with <hi type="italic">Abraham</hi><div eID="gen97669" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.13.28" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen97668" osisID="Luke.13.28" type="section"/>
entries.ad926704bac6276afcf362765e635b4a79577e35:
29. And they shall come from the east He now draws a larger illustration from the fact, that the Jews, who reckoned themselves the only lawful heirs of God, were to be rejected, and that the Gentiles were to be substituted in their room, and obtain the life which was promised to Abraham and his posterity. He contrasts the Gentiles with them, in order to excite them to faith by a holy jealousy: as Paul writes, that
“it will be a distinguished honor of his ministry, if he excite any of his nation and blood to such an emulations,” (Romans 11:13,14.)
The Jews must have been stung by it: for they had an inordinate love of themselves, and proudly despised God and his gifts. But as we shall, ere long, meet with this sentence again in the Gospel by Matthew I now glance at it more slightly.
entries.7d656f74c50b0a629e6e5f364eeae9c8a2f516d5:
30. And, lo, they are last who shall be first The same words, as we shall elsewhere see, were frequently employed by Christ, but in a different sense, (Matthew 19:30; 20:16; Mark 10:31.) All that he intended here was, to throw down the vain confidence of the Jews, who, having been chosen by God in preference to all the rest of the world, trusted to this distinction, and imagined that God was in a manner bound to them. For this reason, Christ threatens that their condition will soon be changed; that the Gentiles, who were at that time cast off, would obtain the first rank; and that the Jews, deprived of their honor, would not even occupy the farthest corner in the Church.
“Ne tiendront pas mesme le dernier reng, ou quelque petit coin en l'Eglise;” — “will not hold even the lowest rank, or some small corner in the Church.”
MATTHEW 7:15-20; LUKE 6:43-45
Matthew 7:15-20
Luke 6:43-45
15. But beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves. 16. From their fruits you shall know them. Do men gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles? 17. So every good tree yields good fruits, and a rotten tree yields bad fruits. 18. A good tree cannot yield evil fruits, nor can a rotten tree yield good fruits. 19. Every tree, which does not yield good fruit, is cut down, and is thrown into the fire. 20. Therefore from their fruits you shall know them.
43. For the tree is not good which yields rotten fruit; and the tree is not rotten which yields good fruit. 44. For every tree is known from its fruit: for men do not gather figs from thorns, nor from thorns do they gather grapes. 45. A good man, out of the good treasure of his heart, bringeth forth what is good, and a bad man, out of the bad treasure of his heart, bringeth forth what is bad. entries.2f8ab66f55564fff0c70ae4e32b970405ea049cf: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.13.31" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.13.31" sID="gen99480" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99481" type="x-p"/>It deserves our attention, that Christ gives the designation, <hi type="italic">daughter of Abraham,</hi> to one whose body had been <hi type="italic">enslaved by Satan during eighteen years. </hi>She was so called, not only in reference to her lineage, as all the Jews without exception gloried in this title, but because she was one of the true and actual members of the Church. Here we perceive also what Paul tells us, that some are<div eID="gen99481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99482" type="x-p"/>delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus, <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.5.5">1 Corinthians 5:5</reference>.)<div eID="gen99482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99483" type="x-p"/>And the length of time points out to us that, though the Lord does not immediately relieve our distresses, yet we ought not to despair.<div eID="gen99483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99484" type="x-p"/>It is difficult to ascertain the precise time when this happened, farther than that Christ was at that time residing in Galilee, as during the whole period of his public calling he remained longer there than in any other place. Certain persons, wishing to be considered as his friends, advise him that, if he wishes to be in safety, he should go beyond the boundaries of Herod’s jurisdiction. In what manner those who gave that advice were affected towards him we have no means of knowing; but I am strongly inclined to conjecture, that they attempted to drive him to some other place, because they saw that the greater part of the people in that place were attached to Christ, so that the Gospel was generally received. We must observe who those advisers were. Luke says that they were <hi type="italic">some of the Pharisees</hi> Now we know that that sect was not so favorable to Christ as to make it probable that those men were anxious about his life. What then? Their design was, to awaken in him such fears as would drive him to some place of concealment; for they expected that, in a short time, his authority would decline, and that his whole doctrine would vanish away. But we must also direct our attention to the first originator and contriver of this scheme, Satan; for, as he endeavored at that time to interrupt the progress of the Gospel, by terrifying the Son of God, so he constantly invents and hatches up new grounds of alarm, to strike the ministers of Christ with dismay, and to constrain them to turn aside.<div eID="gen99484" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.13.31" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99480" osisID="Luke.13.31" type="section"/>
entries.90468d44aadeeb0b2328958387f8ce538e770cc4: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.13.32" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.13.32" sID="gen99485" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99486" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">32. </hi><hi type="italic">Go, tell that fox</hi> It is certain, that the person here spoken of is Herod Antipas. Though he had throughout the character of a <hi type="italic">fox, </hi>and was as remarkable for servility as for cunning, I do not think that the term, <hi type="italic">fox, </hi>is intended to refer generally to the cunning of his whole life, but rather to the insidious methods by which he labored to undermine the doctrine of the Gospel, when he did not venture to attack it openly. Christ tells him that, with all his craftiness, he will gain nothing by his schemes. “Whatever artifices he may devise,” says Christ, “<hi type="italic">today and tomorrow</hi> I will discharge the office which God has enjoined upon me; and when I shall have reached the end of my course, I shall then be offered in sacrifice.” That we may perceive more clearly the meaning of the words, Christ acknowledges, in the former part of his message, that on <hi type="italic">the third </hi>day—that is, within a very short time—he must die; and in this way shows, that he could not be deterred from his duty by any fear of death, to which he advanced boldly, with fixed purpose of mind.<div eID="gen99486" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.13.32" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99485" osisID="Luke.13.32" type="section"/>
entries.c358c24d963dff29efb736cddc9b1a714c5bc793:
33. It does not usually happen, etc. He next adds, that it is an idle bugbear, which is held out by false and hypocritical advisers; because there is no danger of death anywhere else than at Jerusalem. In this second clause he sharply attacks the Pharisees. “Is it you, who — I foresee — will be my executioners, that advise me to beware of Herod?” The reproof extends, indeed, much farther; for he says, not only that preparations had been made for his own death in Jerusalem, but that it might be said to have been, for a long period, a den of robbers, in which almost all the prophets had been murdered. Many had, no doubt, been slain in other places, and particularly at the time when that cruel fury,
“Cette cruelle diablesse;” — “that cruel female devil.”
Jezebel, (1 Kings 19:2,) raged against them; but because in no other place had the prophets, at any time, been fiercely tormented, Christ justly brings this reproach against the ungodly inhabitants of the holy city.
It usually happened that the prophets were slain there; because not only was it the source of all the ungodliness which spread over the whole of Judea, but it was also the field on which God trained his prophets.
“Auquel Dieu a voulu que ses Prophetes ayent soustenu de grans combats et rudes alarmes;” — “on which God determined that his Prophets should sustain powerful combats and fierce alarms.”
We know that the more brightly the light of doctrine shines, so as to press more closely on wicked men, they are driven to a greater pitch of madness. What a dreadful example was it, that a place which had been chosen to be the sanctuary of divine worship, and the residence of the Law and of heavenly wisdom, should be polluted not by one or another murder,, but by a regular butchery of the prophets! It undoubtedly shows how obstinate is the rebellion of the world in rejecting sound doctrine.
The exclamation which immediately follows in Luke, (13:34,) appears to be connected in such a manner, as if Christ had taken occasion from the present occurrence to inveigh, at this time, against Jerusalem But for my own part, I rather think, that Luke, having said that Jerusalem had been formerly stained by the blood of the prophets, nay, had been, through an uninterrupted succession of many ages, the slaughter-place, where the prophets were cruelly and wickedly put to death, immediately inserts, according to his custom, a statement which harmonized with that discourse. We have seen, on former occasions, that it is by no means unusual with him to introduce into one place a collection of Christ’s sayings, which were uttered at various times.
Luke 11:37-41
Luke 11:37-41
37. And while he was speaking, a certain Pharisee requested him to dine with him; and he entered and sat down at table. 38. And when the Pharisee saw it, he wondered that he had not first washed before dinner. 39. And the Lord said to him, Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the plate; and what is within you is full of cruelty and wickedness. 40. Fools, did not he who made what is without make also what is within? 41. But out of what you have
“Des choses presentes, ou, de ce que vous avez;” —”of present things, or, of what you have.”
give alms; and, lo, all things are clean to you.

               <ns0:p n="1">1 THere were present at that season, some that told him of the Galileans, whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 And Jesus answering, said unto them, Suppose ye that these Galileans were sinners above all the Ga<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lileans, because they suffered such things?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 I tell you, Nay: but except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 Or those eighteen upon whom the tower in Si<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />loam fell, and slew them, think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem?<ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>Debtors.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 I tell you, Nay: but except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.<ns0:note place="bottom">The Holy Scriptures giving us no account of these two stories, to which our Saviour doth here refer, and those who have wrote the History of the Jews having given us no account of them, Interpreters are at a great loss to determine any thing about them; we read of one <ns0:hi>Iudas of Galilee,</ns0:hi> who drew away much People after him<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and perished, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 5.37. It is said, that h<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> seduced People from their obedience to the <ns0:hi>Roman Emperor,</ns0:hi> perswading them not to acknowledge him as their Governour, nor to pay tribute to the <ns0:hi>Romans.</ns0:hi> It is guessed by Interpreters, that some of this Faction coming up to the <ns0:hi>Passover,</ns0:hi> (for they were Jews) <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> fell upon them, and slew them while they were sacrificing. Others think that these were some remnant of <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> his Faction, but <ns0:hi>Samaritanes,</ns0:hi> and slain while they were sacrificing at their Temple in Mount <ns0:hi>Gerazim,</ns0:hi> and that (tho <ns0:hi>Samaritanes</ns0:hi>) they were called <ns0:hi>Galileans,</ns0:hi> because <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> the head of their Faction was such. The <ns0:hi>Reader</ns0:hi> is at liberty to chuse which of these he thinks most probable, for I find no other account given by any. The latter is prejudiced by our Saviour<ns0:hi>'s</ns0:hi> calling them <ns0:hi>Galileans,</ns0:hi> and advantaged by the desperate hatred which the Jews had to the <ns0:hi>Samaritanes,</ns0:hi> which might make them more prone to censure any passages of Divine Providence severe towards them. But what the certain crime, or provocation was, we cannot say; we are sure that <ns0:hi>de facto</ns0:hi> the thing was true, <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> did mingle the Blood of some <ns0:hi>Galileans</ns0:hi> with their sacrifices, of which a report was brought to Christ. We are at the same loss for those <ns0:hi>eighteen upon whom the Tower of</ns0:hi> Siloam <ns0:hi>fell. Siloe</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Siloa</ns0:hi> was the name of a small fountain, at the foot of Mount <ns0:hi>Zion,</ns0:hi> which as we are told did not constantly, but at certain times send out Waters, which running through hollow places of the Earth, and Mines and Quarries of Stone made agreat noise. <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> mentions it, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 8.6. There was also a Pool in <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> which had that name, and had a Wall built by it, <ns0:hi>Neh.</ns0:hi> 3.15. Christ sent the Blind Man to go and wash there, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 9.7. <ns0:hi>Turrets</ns0:hi> are (as we know) very usual upon Walls. It seems one of these <ns0:hi>Towers</ns0:hi> fell, and slew eighteen Persons, come thither either to wash themselves, or by reason of some healing vertue in those Waters, upon what occasion we cannot determine. But there they perished. This Story seems to have been something older than the other. Our Saviour either had heard, what some People had said, or at least knew what they would say upon those accidents, (for we are mightily prone to pass uncharitable Judgments upon Persons perishing suddenly, especially if they dye by a violent Death.) As he therefore took all occasions to press upon them <ns0:hi>Repentance,</ns0:hi> so he doth not think fit to omit one so fair, and tho he doth not by what he saith, for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bid us to observe such extraordinary Providences, and to whom they happen, but willeth us to hear, and fear; yet he tells them, there were many <ns0:hi>Galileans,</ns0:hi> as bad as they, who unless they re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pented (that is) being sensible of, heartily turned from the wickedness of their ways, would perish also; thereby teaching us, 1. That punishments come upon People for their Sins, and more signal punishments, for more signal Sinnings. 2. That altho God sometimes by his Providence signally punisheth some for notorious Sinnings, yet he spareth more such Sinners then he so signally punisheth. 3. That therefore none can conclude from such signal punishments, that such Persons punished, were greater Sinners then they. 4. That the best use we can make of such reports, and spectacles of notorious Sinners, more than ordinarily punish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, is to examine our selves, and to repent lest we also perish.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 He spake also this parable, <ns0:note place="margin">Math. 21.19.</ns0:note> A certain man had a fig-tree planted in his vine-yard, and he came and sought fruit thereon, and found none.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 Then said he unto the dresser of his vineyard, Behold, these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig-tree, and find none, cut it down, why cumbreth it the ground?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 And he answering, said unto him, Lord, let it alone this year also, till I shall dig about it and dung <ns0:hi>it.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 And if it bear fruit, <ns0:hi>well</ns0:hi>: and if not, <ns0:hi>then</ns0:hi> after that, thou shalt cut it down.<ns0:note place="bottom">This Parable very <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>itly cohereth with the preceding discourse, there he had let his hearers know; that tho God spareth some Sinners, and hath a longer patience with them, then others, tho they be every whit as great transgressors, in expectation still that they should bring forth fruit; yet if they answer not the means which God useth with them to bring them to repentance, they shall not be spared long, but vengeance shall overtake them also. Those who think that this Parable concerned not the Jews only, but all Mankind, or more especially those who are in the pale of the Church, judge well, provided that they allow it to have been spoken with a primary reference to that Nation, amongst whom Christ had now been Preaching and Working Miracles three years, and expected the fruits of Repentance, and Reformation from them in vain. I do not think it any prejudice to this, that the Vine<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dresser begged but for one year longer, whereas after this Christ had patience with them forty years, before they were destroyed, for <ns0:hi>one year</ns0:hi> may not be intended strictly, (tho the <ns0:hi>three years be</ns0:hi>) but to signify some little time more, that the A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />postles might use all probable means to reclaim them, and make them more fruitful. <ns0:hi>Grotius</ns0:hi> thinks the term of <ns0:hi>three years</ns0:hi> is used, because every figtree (not wholly barren) brought forth fruit one year in three, which notion (if true) of that plant is valuable, but may be of ill consequence, if any should thence conclude, that Mens days of Grace exceed not three years; yet thus much is observable, that when God sends a faithful Minister to a place, the greatest success and blessing of their Ministry is within a few of their first years in a place. The Parable doubtless extend<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth much further than to the People of the Jews, and learns us all these lessons. 1. That where God plants any one within the pale of his Church, he looks<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> he or she should bring forth the fruits of Repentance and Faith. 2. That many are so planted, yet bring forth no fruit. 3. That there is a determined time beyond which God will not bear with barren Souls. 4. That barren Souls a<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e not only useless, but also spoil others <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, they make the soil unprofitable, a <ns0:hi>quench coal</ns0:hi> spoils the fire. 5. That faithful Ministers, will be very earnest with God to spare even barren Souls. 6. That it is their work and duty to use all probable means to make barren Souls fruitful. <ns0:hi>I will dig about it, and dung it.</ns0:hi> 7. That a bearing fruit at last will save Souls from ruin, and destruction. 8. That without it, every Soul tho standing in Gods vineyard, will at last perish eternally.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 And he was teaching in one of the synagogues on the sabbath.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 And behold, there was a woman which had a spirit of infirmity eighteen years, and was bowed together, and could in no wise lift up <ns0:hi>her self.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 And when Jesus saw her, he called <ns0:hi>her</ns0:hi> to him, and said unto her, Woman, thou art loosed from thine infirmity.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 And he laid <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> hands on her: and immediately she was made straight, and glorified God.<ns0:note place="bottom">Tho the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> be <ns0:hi>in the Sabbaths,</ns0:hi> which might signifie any day of the Week, yet it is manifest by what followeth that this Miracle was wrought upon the Seventh day, which was the Jewish Sabbath, else the Ruler of the Synagogue would not have quarrelled with our Saviour about it. What is meant here <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 11. by a <ns0:hi>Spirit of Infirmity,</ns0:hi> would not easily be determined, whether only a <ns0:hi>very great Infirmity,</ns0:hi> or an Infirmity, in the bringing and conti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nuing of which upon her the <ns0:hi>Devil</ns0:hi> had a great instrumentality, but for <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 16. where she is said to be one that Satan had bound, she was a cripple and so bowed down that she could not lift up her self, and thus she had been for eighteen years, so as the distem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />per was inveterate, and out of the course of ordinary cure. Christ who as to Peoples bodily infirmit<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>es, was sometimes found of those that sought him not, seeing her, calleth her to him, and saith, <ns0:hi>Woman thou art loosed from thy infirmity, He layeth his hands on her, and immediately she was straight.</ns0:hi> The inveterateness of the Disease, and the instantaneousness of the Ear, without the use of any means, made the Miracle evident. The Woman for it gave thanks to God, for that is meant by <ns0:hi>glorified God,</ns0:hi> she spake some things to the honour, and Glory of God who had healed her.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 And the ruler of the synagogue answered with indignation, because that Jesus had healed on the sabbath-day, and said unto the people, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 20.9.</ns0:note> There are six days in which men ought to work: in them there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore come and be healed, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matth. 12.10. Chap. 6.7.</ns0:note> and not on the sabbath-day.<ns0:note place="bottom">Answering here signifies no more then <ns0:hi>he spake,</ns0:hi> as in a multi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tude of other places in the Gospels. The Jews were both very Superstitious, and very uneven, as to the Sanctification of the Sabbaths, <ns0:hi>Superstitious</ns0:hi> because they would not do many things, which by Gods Law they might do, such as applying means to heal the Sick, defending themselves against Enemies, <ns0:hi>&c. Vneven</ns0:hi> because they would do divers things of equal bodily labour, with those things which they pretended to scruple, one of which we shall hear our Saviour by and by instancing in. This Ruler studyed to defame him before the People. His pretence was, this was a <ns0:hi>Work,</ns0:hi> and such a Work, as might be done in the six days. Let us hear how our Saviour defendeth himself.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 The Lord then answered him, and said, Thou hypocrite, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 15.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> doth not each one of you on the sab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bath
<ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:312" />
loose his ox or <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> ass from the stall, and lead <ns0:hi>him</ns0:hi> away to watering?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 And ought not this woman being a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan hath bound, lo these eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the sabbath day?<ns0:note place="bottom">Our Saviour here calleth this Ruler of the Synagogue Hypocrite, for his impudence in so severe a reflection on him for doing on the Sabbath-Day, a Work of that Nature, which he himself did, and thought himself blameless in the doing of, and his friends ordinarily did, upon whom for so working he did not reflect, thereby teaching us one note of an <ns0:hi>Hypocrite, viz. To reflect upon others for things which we do our selves.</ns0:hi> This Ruler of the Synagogue and his Party indeed did not <ns0:hi>heal on the Sabbath Day.</ns0:hi> But what kind of Work was healing? was it not a Work of Mercy? what servile labour was there in it. It is only said Christ called this poor Creature, and <ns0:hi>she came,</ns0:hi> not she was brought to him. What did Christ do? he only laid his hands upon her, and pronounced her loosed from her infirmity. Now the Jews would ordinarily upon the Sabbath-Day, loose a Beast from the Stall, to go and drink at a Pit, or lead it thither, was not this a greater labour? how came this to be Lawful, and not that act of Mercy which Christ did shew to this poor Creature? Their act was capable of no other excuse, then that it was an Act of Mercy, and a good Man will shew Mercy to his Beast; it could be no Act of <ns0:hi>Piety,</ns0:hi> nor of <ns0:hi>Necessity</ns0:hi>; for a Beast may live one Day without Water, or at least might have had Water set by it the Night before; nay our Lords Work of Mercy was much more Noble. Theirs was to a Beast, his to <ns0:hi>one of Mankind,</ns0:hi> to a <ns0:hi>Woman,</ns0:hi> and she a <ns0:hi>Iewish Woman,</ns0:hi> a Daughter of <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> a Father upon whom they much valued themselves, and their whole Nation, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 3.9. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 8.39<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Their Beast might not be Sick, she was under an Infirmity, and that no ordinary Infirmity, she was in the hands of the Enemy of Mankind, <ns0:hi>bound by Satan,</ns0:hi> nor was her affliction of a few days continuance, she had been so bound <ns0:hi>eighteen years.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 And when he had said these things, all his adversaries were ashamed: and all the people re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />joyced for all the glorious things that were done by him.<ns0:note place="bottom">It is one thing to be ashamed, another thing to be convinced, so as to confess an error; they were ashamed, that they were so put to silence before the People, but we read of no confession of their error, and mistake, and begging Christs Pardon, the People re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />joyced and gave thanks to God, for all the glorious things that were done by our Saviour.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 Then said he, Unto what is the kingdom of God like? and whereunto shall I resemble it?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 It is like a grain of Mustard-seed, which a man took and cast into his garden, and it grew, and waxed a great tree: and the fowls of the air lodged in the branches of it.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 And again he said, Whereunto shall I liken the kingdom of God?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 It is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leaven<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 13.31, 32, 33. They are two Pa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rables by which Christ foretelleth the great Success of the Gospel, notwithstanding the present small appearance of the efficacy of it.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matth. 9.35. Mark 6.6.</ns0:note> And he went through the cities, and villages, teaching and journeying towards Jerusalem.<ns0:note place="bottom">Still wherever we find our Blessed Lord, we find him <ns0:hi>teaching,</ns0:hi> and that not by an exemplary Life only, but by Word of Mouth, there are different opinions whether our Saviour was now journey<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing towards <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> with respect to the <ns0:hi>Passover,</ns0:hi> or some other great <ns0:hi>Festival</ns0:hi> of the Jews.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 Then said one unto him, Lord, are there few that be saved? And he said unto them,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 Strive to enter in at the strait gate: for many, I say unto you, will seek to enter in, and shall not be able.<ns0:note place="bottom">Our Saviour hath told us <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 7.13. that <ns0:hi>straight is the way, and narrow is the Gate, that leadeth to eternal Life, and few there be that find it.</ns0:hi> Upon this this exhortation is founded <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> contend, or strive to enter in at this straight Gate, a Word which signifies a labouring against opposition, and the utmost indeavour of the Mind, and Body; not that our own labouring will bring us thither, for <ns0:hi>eternal Life</ns0:hi> is the Gift of God, and without the influence of his Grace, we can do nothing effectually; but to let us know, that the Lord will give Heaven, to none but such as labour, and strive for it, yea and also <ns0:hi>strive lawfully,</ns0:hi> he tells us that many shall <ns0:hi>seek and shall not enter.</ns0:hi> Either seeking in a wrong way, or in an undue time. By this Speech of our Saviours he diverts them from that curious Question, about the number of those that shall be saved. That was not so much their concern to know, as that they should be some of that Number.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 When once the master of the house is risen up, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matth. 25.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> hath shut to the door, and ye begin to stand without, and to knock at the door, saying, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 6.4<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> Lord, Lord, open unto us; and he shall answer, and say unto you, I <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Math. 25.12</ns0:note> know you not whence you are.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 Then shall ye begin to say, We have eaten and drunk in thy presence, and thou hast taught in our streets.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 But he shall say, I tell you, I know you not whence you are; <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 6.8. Math. 25.41.</ns0:note> depart from me all ye workers of iniquity.<ns0:note place="bottom">Our Saviour in these verses doth represent himself by a Man, who having invited guests to his Supper, stays till all those who were invited, and accepted the invitation were come in; then rising up, shuts the Door, and after that is shut, turns a deaf ear to any that shall come knocking, let them plead for admittance what they can plead. By this Parabolical expressing of himself, he both openeth in part, what he meant by the foregoing Words. <ns0:hi>Many shall seek to enter in, and shall not enter,</ns0:hi> and also lets us know, that there is a determinate time, wherein Souls must (if ever) accept of the offers of Grace and Salvation, when they are made to them, which if they slip, they will not be able to obtain of God an entrance into the Kingdom of Heaven. <ns0:hi>Seek the Lord while he may be found,</ns0:hi> saith the Prophet, <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> 55.6.7. <ns0:hi>In an acceptable time I have heard thee,</ns0:hi>) saith the Prophet) <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> 49.8. which the Apostle, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 6.2. applyeth to perswade Men, that they should not receive the <ns0:hi>Grace of God</ns0:hi> (in the Gospel) <ns0:hi>in vain,</ns0:hi> what this determinate time is, God hath hidden from us, and it is probable that it is not the same as to all Persons, we know nothing to the contrary, but while there is life there is hope, which warranteth us to Preach Faith and Repentance to all. We are also further instructed. <ns0:hi>That no outward Priviledges,</ns0:hi> tho Christ <ns0:hi>hath taught in our Streets. No external acts of Communion with Christ,</ns0:hi> tho we can say, <ns0:hi>we have Eat and Drunk with him,</ns0:hi> will justifie our hopes of entrance into Heaven, if in the mean time, we be <ns0:hi>workers of iniquity,</ns0:hi> we had much the same, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 7.21, 22, 23. See the Notes there.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when ye shall see Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, and you <ns0:hi>your selves</ns0:hi> thrust out.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 And they shall come from the east, and <ns0:hi>from</ns0:hi> the west, and from the north, and <ns0:hi>from</ns0:hi> the south, and shall sit down in the kingdom of God.<ns0:note place="bottom">We have the same <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 8.11, 12. only he saith, only <ns0:hi>from the East, and from the West.</ns0:hi> See the Notes there, <ns0:hi>wailing, and gnashing of teeth,</ns0:hi> are usual expressions by which the pains of the Damned are expressed, especially by the Evangelist <ns0:hi>Matthew, ch.</ns0:hi> 8.12. <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 13.42.50. <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 22.13. <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 24.51. <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 25.30. One cause of this vexation of Spirit expressed under this Notion, is the Jews sight of the rest and happiness that their Relations, nay some to whom they upon Earth were Enemies, should enjoy in Heaven. Nay which some which were <ns0:hi>Heathens</ns0:hi> should enjoy there, when as they took themselves to be the only Church, and to have the same right to the Kingdom of Heaven, that Children have to the Inheritances of their Father, should he cast out, as having no por<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion there.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 And behold, there are last which shall be first, and there are first which shall be last.<ns0:note place="bottom">This is a Sentence which our Saviour often made use of and not always to the same purpose. See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 19.30 <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 20.16. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 10.31. As to the sense of them here it is plain. Our Saviour here foretelleth the Conversion of the <ns0:hi>Gentiles,</ns0:hi> but yet I do not take the Gentiles to be all who are intended under the Notion of <ns0:hi>the Last,</ns0:hi> but divers others also. Men who both in their opinion of themselves, and in reality with respect to Privi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge, are <ns0:hi>the first,</ns0:hi> whether in respect of <ns0:hi>Gifts,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Office,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>the means of Grace,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Profession,</ns0:hi> will many of them be <ns0:hi>the last,</ns0:hi> that is, furthest off from the Kingdom of God; and many <ns0:hi>who are the last,</ns0:hi> upon these accounts will in the Day of Judgment <ns0:hi>be first,</ns0:hi> that is, appear so, as having more of the favour of God, and be so, taken to Heaven, when the others shall be cast to Hell, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 11.20, 21, 22, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 The same day there came certain of the Pha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />risees, saying unto him, Get thee out, and depart hence: for Herod will kill thee.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 And he said unto them, Go ye and tell that fox, Behold, I cast out devils, and I do cures to day and to morrow, and the third day I shall be perfect<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 Nevertheless, I must walk to day and to mor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />row, and the day following: for it cannot be that a prophet perish out of Jerusalem.<ns0:note place="bottom">It is plain from this Text, that our Saviour was at this time in <ns0:hi>Galilee,</ns0:hi> for that was the <ns0:hi>Tetrachy</ns0:hi> or Province of <ns0:hi>Herod Antipa<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>,</ns0:hi> who is the <ns0:hi>Herod</ns0:hi> here mentioned; whether these <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> came upon their own heads, or as sent by <ns0:hi>Herod</ns0:hi> is not so plain, nor so well agreed by <ns0:hi>Interpreters.</ns0:hi> If they came upon their own heads, it is certain they came not out of kindness, for the whole History of the Gospel, lets us know, that the <ns0:hi>Pharisees,</ns0:hi> had no kindness for Christ, but were his most implacable Enemies, and continually consulting how to destroy him, but they either came to scare him out of <ns0:hi>Galilee,</ns0:hi> whose repute was so great, and who did them so much mischief there, or to drive him into the <ns0:hi>trap,</ns0:hi> which they had laid for him in <ns0:hi>Iudea.</ns0:hi> But it is most probable, that they came as secretly sent by <ns0:hi>Herod,</ns0:hi> who tho of himself he be reported to be of no Bloody disposition, yet upon the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> continual sollicitations might be perswaded, to send them on this errand, chusing rather cunningly to scare him out of his Province, then by violence to fall upon him. This opinion looks more probable, because <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 32. Our Saviour sends them back with a Message to <ns0:hi>Herod, Go and tell that Fox. Herod</ns0:hi> had gained himself no re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />putation amongst the Jews, by his Murthering <ns0:hi>Iohn the Baptist,</ns0:hi> whom the Jews generally valued as a <ns0:hi>Prophet,</ns0:hi> and probably seeing our Saviour exceeding him in popular applause, he was not willing to augment the <ns0:hi>Odium,</ns0:hi> which already lay upon him for that Fact, yet to gratifie the <ns0:hi>Pharisees,</ns0:hi> (many of which were in his Province) he was willing if he could effect it cleaverly, and without noise, to be quit of Christ, especially considering (as we before heard) he had an opinion, that he was <ns0:hi>Iohn Baptist risen from the Dead,</ns0:hi> or the Soul of <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Baptist</ns0:hi> in another Body, and possibly he could not tell what might be the effect of his Ghost, so haunting his <ns0:hi>Province.</ns0:hi> It is certain, that either he, or the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> or both had a mind to have him gone some whither else, to which purpose this Message is brought to him. Our Saviour either dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerning <ns0:hi>Herods craft</ns0:hi> in this thing, or having observed the craft he used in the whole managery of his Government, that he might keep favour both with the <ns0:hi>Roman Emperor,</ns0:hi> and with the Jews, bids them, <ns0:hi>Go and tell that Fox.</ns0:hi> I do not much value their Critical observation, who observe that it is not <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> but <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> that is, <ns0:hi>this Fox,</ns0:hi> from whence they would observe that our Saviour might mean the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> not <ns0:hi>Herod,</ns0:hi> nor is there any need of it to excuse our Saviour, from the violation of that Law of God, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 22.28. <ns0:hi>Thou shalt not revile the Gods, nor curse the Ruler of thy People,</ns0:hi> which Law <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> reflected on, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 23.5. and pleads ignorance for his calling <ns0:hi>Ananias, a white Wall.</ns0:hi> For we shall observe that the Prophets all along (being immediately sent from God) took a further liberty then any o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers, in severely reproving <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Princes. Elijah</ns0:hi> tells <ns0:hi>Ahab</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> was <ns0:hi>he that troubled Israel,</ns0:hi> the Prophets call the Rulers of the Jews<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>Rulers of Sodom,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Princes of Gomorrha, &c.</ns0:hi> But Christ may be allowed a liberty neither Lawful, nor decent for other Persons, no tho they were Prophets. But what is the message which Christ sends by these Pharisees? <ns0:hi>Behold I cast out Devils, and I do cures to day, and to Morrow, and the third day I shall be perfected.</ns0:hi> Tell him saith he what I am doing, I am freeing his Subjects from molestations by evil Spirits, and the in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cumbrances of many Diseases. What do I do worthy of Death? I have but a little time to trouble him, for in a little time I must Dye, which is that which he means by being <ns0:hi>perfected,</ns0:hi> it is plain that those Words <ns0:hi>to Day,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>to Morrow,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>third Day,</ns0:hi> must not be taken strictly, for Christ lived more then three Days after this. If this will not satisfie him, tell him, (saith our Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viour.) That <ns0:hi>I must walk to Day and to Morrow, and the Day following.</ns0:hi> I know, that as to this thing I am not under his Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mand, or Power, <ns0:hi>I must walk,</ns0:hi> &c. My Days are not in his hands, and I know that <ns0:hi>he cannot kill me, for it cannot be that a Prophet perish out of Ierusalem. Ierusalem</ns0:hi> is the place where I must die, not <ns0:hi>Galilee</ns0:hi>; the Sanhedrim sits at <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> who alone can take cognisance of the <ns0:hi>case</ns0:hi> of false <ns0:hi>Prophets,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> is the place where the People must fill up the measure of their ini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quities by spilling my Blood. Upon this our Saviour breaketh out into a <ns0:hi>sad Lamentation</ns0:hi> of the case of that once <ns0:hi>Holy City,</ns0:hi> the praise of the whole Earth.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="34">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:313" />34 O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent unto thee: how often would I have gathered thy children toge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, as a hen <ns0:hi>doth gather</ns0:hi> her brood under <ns0:hi>her</ns0:hi> wings, and ye would not?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="35">35 Behold, your house is left unto you desolate: And verily I say unto you, Ye shall not see me, until the time come when ye shall say, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psa. 118.26.</ns0:note> Blessed <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> he that cometh in the name of the Lord.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 23<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 37, 38, 39. These five last verses afford us much for our instruction. 1. We may from them learn the <ns0:hi>craft</ns0:hi> of the Enemies of the Gospel, as well as their Malice, they are <ns0:hi>Lions,</ns0:hi> and will like <ns0:hi>Lions</ns0:hi> tear and rend, when they see an opportunity; but when they see it convenient, then they put on the <ns0:hi>fox's skin,</ns0:hi> doing the same thing by subtilty, which they durst not attempt to effect by cruelty. 2. Their <ns0:hi>Malice</ns0:hi> is as much perspicuous; who but the Children of the Devil could have found in their hearts, to have desired Christ to go out of their Country, who did nothing there, but innocently, and diligently Preach the Gospel, deliver People from grievous Diseases, and the Power of <ns0:hi>Satan,</ns0:hi> who miserably possest and tormented them? 3. When the most Malicious Enemies of Gods People have done what they can, they shall finish their course, and work the time God hath set them. 4. When they have perfected their Work, they shall be perfected. Death is but the perfecting the Saints, as it was the perfecting of Christ. 5. Men shall Dye as at the time, so at the place which God hath set. 6. God sending of his Ministers faithfully to reveal his Will to People, is a declaration of his wil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lingness to gather them under the Wings of his special favour and protection. 7. The perverse Wills of Men, are those things which hinder Men and Women from being gathered. 8. Temporal judg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments, and that of the severest Nature will first or last follow Mens contempt of the offers of Grace and Salvation. 9. Those that do contemn the means of Grace, shall not see them long.—<ns0:hi>Ye shall not see me.</ns0:hi> 10. The Proudest Scorners and Contemners of Christ and his Grace, shall one Day wish, that one would or might come unto them in the Name of the Lord, and do but now contemn what hereafter they would be glad they might enjoy.</ns0:note>
